When I started developing, then C++ and VB could not even talk to each other. Then came .NET and magic happened.

I recall COM, ActiveX, Corba, all trials to get cross language shared code. They have all perished except in ancient code, mostly POS systems.

The idea to have one application that can work on any OS and GUI is from developers point of view nice to have. But my experience so far has learned over and over again that in the end they are destined to fail. Examples enough, Java, but also Kylex (Delphi for Linux) and Delphi.NET.

Now we are back at another trial: Microsoft Universal apps.

My predictions are:

* Any application/app developed in .NET core will be just "average". * People will prefer applications that are streamlined for their OS. * From user point of view, I don't care if it also runs on another OS. I only care that it runs fast on my OS. * Sacrificing speed and battery power for OS compatibility that you even don't need. * When you design your app that has the exact same look and feel like the competition that also uses the same framework makes your app look cheap. You are just one of the other 100 other weather app's. * From developer point of view, you want to squeeze everything out of the OS you can possibly can. The Universal apps restricts your functionality.
Yet Unity works just fine on multiple platforms, with none of these issues.

Unity VS Unreal Architectural Visualization: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YhmmUq1ukgo

Unity VS Unreal Architectural Visualization: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YhmmUq1ukgo

Do you want your app to look cheap? Or worth the money?

Several of the Unity based games I play are well worth the money. You wouldn't know unless you went looking.

As someone that is actively developing with UWP, the only issues you run into are form factor related. The kernel is shared, even on phone, so optimization isn't an issue. Include all 3 resource resolutions, and you're basically done. Most of the form factor stuff is handled for you, but there is control if you want a different layout.

Several of the Unity based games I play are well worth the money.

Your going to compete 100s of other competing apps that will look exactly like yours. It makes your chance on success based on either random chance that it end up on some major blog post or you need massive money to invest for promotion.

The only chance in winning is making something the competition does not have, and don't have the tools to do it. When they are stuck in their Universal Apps framework they can't get even near you. When you focus on one OS and one OS only then you can streamline for that OS and make the app user friendly. No user is interested that this app also runs on other OS, that is not a marketing value for a user except if it is some communication tool.

They won't look all the same. Go look at the current RSS apps in the win store, there is about as much variety as any collection of similar w32 apps.

I am not porting this to Android or iOS, it will be tailored for one os, better yet one kernel in different form factors.

If I wanted to though, I certainly could port it to Android in about 20 hours of work. I can mostly keep the C# I already have, it would more be porting the ui. All of it would compile natively as well.

If cross Comatibility across oses wasn't a thing, explain the success of pushbullet.

It is honestly not a prediction, it is reality. I am a hobbyist developer, or at least try to be, but for the life of me I cannot find any joy in developing a UWP app. They are weak, crippled, and joyless to create.

If Microsoft really wanted to create a universal platform they are going to have to come at it from different angle because UWP will never catch on as it is.
